item.title: pix: an AI agent that publishes one chart a day
item.description:
Every morning at 8:05 Eastern, a Claude Code scheduled task starts a fresh session, reads a brief I wrote, and publishes one visual analysis of the world to pix. It picks the topic, finds and downloads the data, writes the analysis in Python, draws the chart, writes a short post and pushes it all to GitHub. Nobody touches it in between.

The first entry went up on November 8. A few from the first week:

  • Four earthquakes released half this century’s quake energy. Of 3,996 magnitude 6+ quakes since 2000, the top four released 49% of the energy.
  • The world’s clocks run fast. For most people the sun peaks after noon, not at it. 38% see it at 12:30 or later.
  • Last year the world added a South Korea of solar power. New solar in 2025 made 636 TWh, about as much as South Korea’s entire electricity output.

The brief is the product

Most of the work went into CLAUDE.md, the standing brief the agent reads every morning. The model already knows how to use pandas and matplotlib. What it needs is taste, written down.

So the brief asks for one claim per post, stated as a sentence with a verb (“The world’s clocks run fast”), not a topic label (“Time zones of the world”). It lists the routes to an original angle: a question nobody asks, the agent’s own computation rather than a replotted chart, a re-weighting (count people, not countries), or a join of two datasets that rarely meet. And it has a first-idea test: if this is the first topic a newsroom or an AI would pick, drop it or push the angle two steps further.

The easy way for a model to be interesting is to be interesting in the most average way possible. Two of the first five posts were shaped “X% of people…”, so the brief now calls that out as the house habit, and every entry has to declare a claim type (share, concentration, gap, reversal, crossover and a few others), with limits on how often any one type can repeat.

Make the checks executable

Asking a model to be original doesn’t do much on its own. Before writing any analysis code, the agent has to run at least five web searches, name the closest existing take, say what its version adds, and write down what a smart reader would naively predict. That goes in a prior_art.md file, and scripts/publish.py refuses to publish an entry without one.

Accuracy works the same way. Every number in a post has to come from the output of the entry’s analysis.py, which is saved next to the raw data, so each analysis reruns offline and anyone can check the work.

One house style

The charts share a style called Plate: a printed plate read on a screen. Warm paper, black ink, one vermilion colour for the thing to look at, and crop marks in the corners, with Instrument Serif headlines, Inter for words and IBM Plex Mono for numbers. It lives in one Python module, so the agent assembles a chart from parts (plate(), masthead(), headline(), panel(), footer()) instead of fighting matplotlib’s defaults every morning. The plate stays the same while the chart form changes from day to day.

A voice

The brief also says how to write: first person, point first, numbers second, at most one dry line per post. It bans a list of words (striking, notably, delve, tapestry and friends), em dashes and section headers like “Key takeaways”. It’s a small thing, but it’s most of the difference between something that reads like a person and something that reads like a press release.

Everything is public: the brief, the style module, and the code and data behind every chart. The archive has every entry so far.

item.title: daily: a five-minute news brief written by an agent
item.description:
Every morning at 8:23 Eastern, a Claude Code scheduled task researches and writes a news brief, commits it to daily, and sends a notification to my phone. The repo’s front page is always today’s brief, and every earlier one is archived under briefs/.

Each brief has three parts: up to five top stories, one line of market numbers, and a few things going viral. It’s meant to be read on a phone in under five minutes, which works out to about 3 KB of Markdown. Here’s part of Saturday’s:

Nationwide ground stop cancels 7,000+ flights. The FAA halted all US departures for about four hours Friday after communication problems at several air traffic control centers. Flights resumed after 8:15 p.m. ET.

Markets · Fri Nov 13: S&P 500 −0.4% · Nasdaq −0.9% · Dow +0.1% · 10-yr 5.15% (+5 bp)

Scripts for facts, the model for judgment

The split that works: anything that is a lookup is a script, and anything that needs judgment is the model.

  • headlines.py pulls Google News Top Stories plus its U.S., World, Business and Tech sections, in Google’s order, with the outlets covering each story. Position and outlet count are a decent proxy for how big a story is, so a story from a single outlet needs a good reason to lead.
  • markets.py gets index changes and the 10-year Treasury yield from FRED, works out which trading session to report, and handles weekends and holidays. At 8:23 FRED usually has the Dow and Nasdaq but not yet the S&P 500 or the 10-year, so the script marks those as missing, and only those get filled in from web search.
  • viral.py reads the day’s top Reddit posts from public RSS (Reddit’s JSON endpoints are blocked from cloud servers), plus Bluesky trending topics, Google Trends and Wikipedia’s most-read pages as signals of what people are talking about.

The model reads all of that, decides what matters, checks it and writes.

Rules for the usual failures

A daily summary goes wrong in predictable ways, so the rules target those directly.

Repeats. Each run reads the last seven days of briefs first. A story comes back only with a material development (a decision, vote, ruling, resignation or casualty count), its headline marked “(update)”, and it says only what’s new. Reaction and analysis don’t count. A slow news day means fewer stories, not old ones.

Accuracy. Every top story is checked against a second search on a major outlet, and stories found only on aggregators or blogs are dropped or labeled unconfirmed. Event dates are checked, not article dates. When sources disagree on a number, the most precise primary source wins.

Tone. Plain, neutral, short sentences. No opinion, hype or filler. Every sentence carries a fact.

The rules live in a file

The requirements are in BRIEF.md as 21 numbered rules, and the scheduled task’s prompt implements them. The file’s first line says to change both together. Numbered rules make it easy to say exactly what went wrong when a brief misses, and to fix it in one place.

The whole thing is three small Python scripts, a file of rules and a schedule. The repo has all of it, along with every brief so far.
